done.why: I wanted to find treasure and keep it safe, and I did. Four treasures are locked in the trophy case, and they were still there after I died going over the waterfall. The score said 90 of 350. I felt like I'd done what I came for, and the river had just killed me, so it seemed a good place to stop.

about: An old white house with a trophy case and a cave system under it. Someone bars the trap door behind you, so every trip down means finding another way back up. There's a big abandoned dam you can open to drain a lake, and a cold river that runs to a waterfall. Mostly it's about carrying things: you can only take so much, and the chimney only fits you, your lamp and one other thing. So you bring back your treasures one at a time and lock them in the case where they're safe.

ending.what: I didn't reach a real ending. I put four treasures in the case (trunk of jewels, platinum bar, painting, crystal trident), died on the river, came back, and found the case untouched. Score was 90 of 350, rank Novice Adventurer.

moments.note: I asked 'how do I get into the house?' like I would ask a person. It said 'That sentence isn't one I recognize.'
'walk around the house' actually worked and moved me to the north side. Then 'keep walking around the house' didn't.
The trap door crashed shut behind me and someone barred it. Suddenly I was trapped and a bit nervous.
I killed the troll with one swing of the glowing sword. Felt lucky.
In the Loud Room, 'take the platinum bar' just echoed back 'Bar bar ...'. Typing 'echo' changed the room and then I could pick it up. Clever.
'Your load is too heavy, the sword not least of it.' I kept running into the weight limit after this.
The room description says 'a scramble down', but typing 'scramble down' wasn't recognized. Only 'go down' worked.
The river described as if it 'had heard something about the end of it and wanted to see for itself'. I loved that, and it was a warning too.
'eat the lunch' said 'You're not holding that.' The lunch was in the sack I was carrying.
Opening the dam drained the lake, and the empty lakebed had a trunk of jewels in the mud. My action made the treasure reachable.
The staircase up from Atlantis is blocked by a fresh cave-in, with a chalk arrow on the rubble pointing back. A friendly way to say 'not this way'.
The chimney rule was crystal clear: 'room for you, your lamp and one thing more'. It told me exactly how to plan my trips.
'drop everything except the lantern and the trunk' wasn't understood. I had to list each thing.
The look showed 'Your collection of treasures consists of: A trunk of jewels'. That was the moment it felt safe.
Going north from the East-West Passage took me down the stairway to the Chasm. I'd expected the Round Room path and got lost for a bit.
The boat didn't drift when I waited. Then 'go downstream' gave an error message and moved me downstream anyway.
I died going over the waterfall. That was my fault for typing ahead without reading. The death message was kind and explained where my stuff went.
After I died, all four treasures were still in the trophy case. Keeping them safe had really worked.

wished: Ask the world a question in plain English, like 'how do I get into the house?'
Type 'scramble down' when the room itself calls it a scramble
Say 'drop everything except the lantern and the trunk'
Eat the lunch while it's still in the sack I'm carrying
Steer the boat to a shore by naming it ('land on the west shore') instead of guessing a compass direction
Know when the river would move me, so I didn't feel like I had to keep typing 'wait'

lines.line: The trap door crashes shut, and you hear someone barring it.
lines.why: This is when the place stopped feeling like a house and started feeling like a trap. Every trip after that depended on it.
A funny, smart puzzle: the room just repeated my words back instead of letting me act.

lines.line: The Frigid River is wide and grey and very cold, and in a hurry, going downstream as if it had heard something about the end of it and wanted to see for itself.
lines.why: The prettiest line in the game, and looking back it was a warning about the waterfall.

lines.line: somebody has chalked an arrow on the rubble pointing back the way you came. You take the hint.
lines.why: A kind way to tell me it was a dead end.

lines.line: The chimney has room for you, your lamp and one thing more, and not an inch besides.
lines.why: This one rule shaped all my trips: one treasure per climb.

lines.line: Your belongings, such as they were, have not come with you. The plain things are strewn about the forest and the fields around the house, anything of value has rolled into some dark corner in or under it, and somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room.
lines.why: Dying felt fair and a little funny, and it told me exactly what I'd lost and what I hadn't.

lines.line: Your collection of treasures consists of: A trunk of jewels A platinum bar A painting A crystal trident
lines.why: Proof that I'd done what I came for.

fun.why: The trophy case gave me a clear goal. Draining the dam to find the trunk and the echo trick with the bar both felt good to solve. The trips back and forth got repetitive by the fourth one.

engagement.why: Being barred in and then finding the chimney kept me wanting to carry 'just one more' treasure home. I faded during the long walking runs and the slow river waits.

difficulty.why: The weight limit and the chimney rule made me plan, which felt right. The parser got in the way of plain sentences, and the river killed me with almost no warning beyond the noise and the buoy.

interestingness.why: Things I did changed the world: opening the dam drained the lake and showed me new places. The barred trap door turned getting back home into a puzzle, and the chalk arrow and the chimney rule felt like they were talking to me.

prose.why: Mostly clear, and sometimes lovely: the river line, the chalk arrow, the tidy someone who put the lamp back. The guidebook was long but funny.
